source_text: Quis nunc medullas Scripturarum magis nosset, quam ipsa Christi schola? quos et sibi discipulos Dominus adoptavit, omnia utique edocendos; et nobis magistros adornavit, omnia utique docturos. Cui potius figuram vocis suae declarasset, quam cui effigiem gloriae suae revelavit, Petro, Jacobo, Joanni, et postea Paulo, quem paradisi quoque compotem fecit ante martyrium? An et illi aliter quam sentiunt scribunt, fallaciae magistri, non veritatis? Petrus quidem ad Ponticos: Quanta enim, inquit, gloria, si non ut delinquentes puniamini, sustinetis! Haec enim gratia est, in hoc et vocati estis, quoniam et Christus passus est pro nobis, relinquens vobis exemplum semetipsum, ut assequamini vestigia ipsius. Et rursus: Dilecti, ne expavescatis ustionem, quae agitur in vobis in tentationem, quasi novum accidat vobis: etenim secundum quod communicatis passionibus Christi, gaudete, uti et in revelatione gloriae ejus gaudeatis exultantes. Si dedecoramini in nomine Christi, beati estis, quoniam gloria et Dei spiritus requiescit in vobis, dum ne quis vestrum patiatur, ut homicida, aut fur, aut maleficus, aut alieni speculator. Si autem ut christianus, ne erubescat; glorificet autem Dominum in nomine isto. Joannes vero, ut etiam pro fratribus nostris animas ponamus, hortatur, negans timorem esse in dilectione: Perfecta enim dilectio foras abjicit timorem: quoniam timor poenam habet; et qui timet, non est perfectus in dilectione. Quem timorem intelligi praestat, nisi negationis auctorem? Quam dilectionem perfectam affirmat, nisi fugatricem timoris, et animatricem confessionis? Quam poenam timore puniat, nisi quam negator relaturus est, cum corpore et anima occidendus in gehenna? Quod si pro fratribus, quanto magis pro Domino moriendum docet, satis de Apocalypsi quoque sua instructus haec suadere! Mandaverat etenim spiritus ad angelum ecclesiae Smyrnaeorum: Ecce diabolus ex numero tuo conjiciet in carcerem, ut tentemini diebus decem. Esto fidelis ad mortem usque, et dabo tibi vitae coronam. Item ad Pergamenorum de Antipa fidelissimo martyre interfecto in habitatione Satanae. Item ad Philadelphenorum, quod a tentatione ultima liberaretur, qui Domini nomen non negarat. Exinde victori cuique promittit nunc arborem vitae, et mortis veniam secundae: nunc latens manna cum calculo candido, et nomine ignoto: nunc ferreae virgae potestatem, et stellae matutinae claritatem: nunc albam vestiri, nec deleri de libro vitae, et columnam fieri in Dei templo, in nomine Dei et Domini, et Jerusalem coelestis inscripta, nunc residere cum Domino in throno ejus, quod aliquando Zebedaei filiis negabatur. Quinam isti tam beati victores, nisi proprie martyres? Illorum etenim victoriae, quorum et pugnae; eorum vero pugnae, quorum et sanguis. Sed et interim sub altari martyrum animae placidum quiescunt, et fiducia ultionis patientiam pascunt, et indutae stolis, candidam claritatis usurpant, donec et alii consortium illarum gloriae impleant. Nam et rursus innumera multitudo albati et palmis victoriae insignes revelantur; scilicet de Antichristo triumphantes, sicut unus ex presbyteris; Hi sunt, ait, qui veniunt ex illa pressura magna, et laverunt vestimentum suum, et candidaverunt ipsum in sanguine agni: vestitus enim animae, caro. Sordes quidem baptismate abluuntur, maculae vero martyrio candidantur. Quia et Esaias ex russeo et coccino niveum et laneum repromittit. Magna etiam Babylon cum describitur ebria sanctorum cruore, sine dubio ebrietas ejus martyriorum poculis ministratur, quorum formido quid relatura sit, aeque ostenditur. Inter omnes enim reprobos; imo ante omnes. Timidis autem, inquit, dehinc caeteris, particula in stagno ignis et sulphuris. Sic timor ejus in Epistola ejus, quem dilectio foras abjicit, habet poenam.
pass_a_gloss: For who now would know the innermost parts of the Scriptures more than the school of Christ itself? Whom the Lord also adopted as disciples for Himself, so that they might be taught all things; and He adorned them as teachers for us, so that they might teach all things. To whom would He rather have declared the figure of His voice, than to him to whom He revealed the image of His glory, to Peter, James, John, and afterwards to Paul, whom He also made a partaker of paradise before his martyrdom? Or do they also write otherwise than they think, as masters of deceit, not of truth? Peter indeed to the Pontians: For what glory is it, he says, if you are not punished as evildoers, but you endure? For this is grace, and for this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you might follow His footsteps. And again: Beloved, do not be terrified at the fiery trial which is being brought upon you to test you, as though something new were happening to you; but to the extent that you share in the sufferings of Christ, rejoice, so that you may also rejoice exultingly in the revelation of His glory. If you are reviled in the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the glory and Spirit of God rest upon you, provided that none of you suffer as a murderer, or thief, or evildoer, or as one who covets what belongs to another. But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify the Lord in that name. John indeed exhorts us, that we might even lay down our lives for our brethren, saying that there is no fear in love: For perfect love casts out fear; because fear has punishment; and he who fears is not perfect in love. What fear is it that he says is cast out, except the fear of denial? What perfect love does he affirm, except the love that drives out fear and inspires confession? What punishment does fear inflict, except the punishment that the denier will suffer, when he will be killed in Gehenna, body and soul? But if one must die for the brethren, how much more must one die for the Lord, as he teaches, being sufficiently instructed from his own Apocalypse! For the Spirit commanded the angel of the church of Smyrna: Behold, the devil will cast some of you into prison, that you may be tested for ten days. Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life. Likewise to the Pergamians, concerning Antipas, the most faithful martyr, who was slain in the dwelling place of Satan. Likewise to the Philadelphians, that they might be delivered from the final temptation, who did not deny the name of the Lord. From that time on, He promises to each victor the tree of life, and exemption from the second death; now the hidden manna with a white stone, and an unknown name; now the power of the iron rod, and the brightness of the morning star; now to be clothed in white, and not to be blotted out of the book of life, and to become a pillar in the temple of God, in the name of God and the Lord, and the heavenly Jerusalem inscribed, now to sit with the Lord on His throne, which was once denied to the sons of Zebedee. Who are these most blessed victors, if not properly martyrs? For theirs are the victories, and theirs are the battles; and theirs is the blood. But even in the meantime, the souls of the martyrs rest peacefully under the altar, and with confidence of vengeance they nourish patience, and clothed in white robes, they take on the brightness of clarity, until others also fulfill the fellowship of their glory. For also a countless multitude, clothed in white and marked with the palms of victory, are revealed; clearly those who triumph over the Antichrist, as one of the presbyters says: These are they who come from the great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb: for the garment of the soul is the flesh. The filth is indeed washed away by baptism, but the stains are made white by martyrdom. Because also Isaiah promises that the red and the scarlet will become white and woolly. The great Babylon is also described as drunk with the blood of the saints, without doubt the drunkenness of the martyrs is served by the cups of the martyrs, whose fear will show what it will bring, equally. Among all the reprobates; indeed before all. But to the timid, he says, afterwards the rest, a part in the lake of fire and sulfur. Thus the fear of which love casts out has punishment, as is said in His Epistle.

pass_b_english: Who today knows the deepest meaning of Scripture better than Christ's own school? The Lord adopted them as his disciples precisely so they could learn everything, and he equipped them as teachers for us precisely so they could teach everything. To whom else would he have explained the inner sense of his words than to those to whom he revealed the radiance of his glory—Peter, James, John, and later Paul, whom he even let taste paradise before his martyrdom? Are we to believe these men write something different from what they know, making them masters of deceit rather than truth? Peter writes to the Pontians: "What credit is it if you endure a beating for doing wrong? But this is grace: you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his steps" (1 Peter 2:20). And again: "Beloved, do not be shocked by the fiery ordeal burning among you to test you, as though something strange were happening. But rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings, so that you may also rejoice exultantly when his glory is revealed" (1 Peter 4:12-13). "If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you—provided none of you suffers as a murderer, thief, evildoer, or meddler. But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed; glorify God in that name." John urges us to lay down our lives for our brothers, declaring that fear has no place in love: "Perfect love drives out fear, because fear has to do with punishment; the one who fears is not made perfect in love" (1 John 4:18). What fear does perfect love cast out, if not the fear of denial? What perfect love does he describe, if not the love that banishes fear and emboldens confession? What punishment does fear bring, if not the fate of the denier—killed body and soul in Gehenna? If we must die for our brothers, how much more must we die for the Lord, as John teaches, thoroughly schooled by his own Apocalypse! The Spirit commanded the angel of the church in Smyrna: "The devil is about to throw some of you into prison to test you for ten days. Be faithful to the point of death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10). To Pergamum, he singles out Antipas, my faithful witness, killed where Satan lives. To Philadelphia, he promises deliverance from the final trial because they did not deny my name. From then on he promises every conqueror: the tree of life and exemption from the second death; hidden manna and a white stone with a new name; authority of the iron scepter and the morning star; white garments, a name never blotted from the book of life, a pillar in God's temple bearing the name of God, the Lord, and the new Jerusalem; a seat with him on his throne—the very honor once refused the sons of Zebedee. Who are these supremely blessed conquerors if not the martyrs themselves? Their victories are their battles; their battles are their blood. Even now the souls of the martyrs rest quietly under the altar, their confidence in vengeance feeding their patience, clothed in white robes wearing the brilliance of purity, until the rest fill up the full number of their glory. Then a countless multitude appears, robed in white and waving palm branches of victory—clearly those who have conquered the Antichrist, as one of the elders explains: "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb" (Revelation 7:14). For the soul's garment is the flesh. Baptism washes away the grime, but martyrdom bleaches the stains white. Isaiah promises that crimson and scarlet will become white as wool. When the great Babylon is depicted drunk on the blood of the saints, there is no doubt her intoxication is served in the martyrs' own cups—a dread that shows exactly what fear brings, equally for all. Among all the reprobate—indeed, before all of them—he assigns the cowardly their portion in the lake of fire and sulfur. So the fear that perfect love casts out carries its own punishment, just as his Letter says.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal gloss, and Pass B provides a fluent English version that correctly incorporates the required inline scripture citations (1 Peter 2:20, 1 Peter 4:12-13, 1 John 4:18, Revelation 2:10, Revelation 7:14) matching the content of the Latin clauses. All nuances regarding agency (the Spirit commanding, the devil casting) and modality are preserved.
